name: Mbara
confidence_why: Goedemans 1998, resting on Breen's 1979 Mbara phonology and Sutton's Yanga-Mbara notes, lists Mbara among the initial-stress languages and Sutton 1973's own transcribed Mbara words carry the accent on the first syllable; the only dissent is Sutton 1973's blanket remark that the region's initial-dropping languages stress a non-initial syllable, which, like Blevins 2001, describes the historical shift onto what is now the first syllable of the word, so the sources are few but do not really conflict.

catalog_quote: Some of the entries have no descriptive source. These must be handled with caution. The stress pattern in these languages was deduced from old scanty material found in the Australian Institute for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS) library and at the Australian National University (ANU). It may be that some of them have been mistakenly placed in a certain category, due to missing crucial information. ... Explanation of codes: ... E: the descriptive source notes many exceptions to the general rule ... ID: the language underwent Initial Dropping ... NMS: No Main Stress, all the stresses in the word are equally strong ... Stress categories / I Main stress on the initial syllable, secondary stress on alternates. (allowance or disallowance of secondary stress on final syllables is not indicated) ... Mbara (T182,3) (ID): Breen, Gavan (1979). Mbara/Yanga vocabulary/ Mbara phonology/ Mbara grammar. Ms, AIATSIS. Sutton, Peter (n.d.). Yanga-Mbara. Ms, AIATSIS.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Goedemans's survey classes Mbara (Tindale T182/183 = Mbara and Yanga) as a language with main stress on the word-initial syllable and secondary stress on alternate syllables thereafter, flagged as having undergone initial dropping; the classification rests on unpublished AIATSIS manuscripts (Breen 1979 'Mbara phonology', Sutton n.d.). Blevins 2001:484 (open, saved) instead lists Yanga and Mbara, citing Sutton 1976, among languages where stress historically 'shifted from first to second syllable, leaving unstressed initial syllables' before initial C-loss; since Sutton 1976 (snippets) lists 'loss of C1V1' among Mbara's developments, the two are reconcilable (old second syllable = present initial syllable), but no first-hand synchronic statement was seen.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Category I implies secondary stress on alternating syllables after the initial main stress; no language-specific detail (no RS/NS/US code given for Mbara).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mbara; Goedemans warns App. D entries deduced from 'old scanty material' at AIATSIS/ANU 'must be handled with caution' and may be misplaced.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level typological classification only; second-hand. Conflicting-looking second-hand diachronic statement in Blevins 2001:484/488 (stress shift to second syllable, source Sutton 1976). Primary Sutton 1976 pp.102-123 could not be opened; its Mbara 'Phonological developments' list (loss of C1V1, metathesis, umlaut, lenition) was seen only in archive.org search snippets without page numbers.
new_statements.identity_note: Goedemans's entry 'Mbara (T182,3)' covers Tindale's two tribes Mbara and Yanga (= Glottolog dialect-level mbar1261 Mbara and yang1308 Yanga under mbar1254); Sutton 1976 treats 'Yanga-Mbara' as mutually intelligible varieties, his own data being Mbara (speakers Chisholm Fred, Norman Clark), Yanga known only from Tindale's vocabulary. Not to be confused with Yangga (Biri dialect) or Mbara of Chad.

new_statements.quote: The languages of north-east Queensland can be roughly divided into two (non-genetic) groupings: 1. a phonologically intact group whose words mostly or always begin with consonants, [...] word-stress on the first syllable and a common minimal word-structure CVCV; and 2. an aberrant group whose words may begin with vowels, which mostly have five or more phonemic vowels, which may have fricatives, complex syllable onsets, word-final stops, word-stress on non-initial syllables, and which have common word-structures VC, VCV, CV, CCVC etc. (p.24) [...] Not only are Mbara and Lama Lama (both aberrant) non-affiliated, but also Yidinj and Njawaygi (both intact). (p.30)

new_statements.relation_note: Nominal contradiction only. The catalog (via Goedemans 1998 App. D category I, from Breen 1979 and Sutton n.d. MSS) records fixed initial stress; Sutton 1973's class-level sentence assigns the aberrant group, which includes Mbara, 'word-stress on non-initial syllables'. That sentence describes the initial-dropping type generally (words that 'may begin with vowels'), not Mbara's own words, and the seven Mbara forms Sutton transcribes with stress marks all carry it on the first (or only) syllable of the consonant-initial modern word, which agrees with the catalog. A 'first post-consonantal vowel' rule and an 'initial syllable' rule give identical results for every Mbara word in this work; the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No Mbara-specific stress rule is stated. Mbara is a 'neighbour' in this Gugu-Badhun thesis and is explicitly placed in the phonologically 'aberrant' (initial-dropping) class, which Sutton characterises as a class by 'word-stress on non-initial syllables' as against the intact class's 'word-stress on the first syllable'. §2.7.2 (p.63-66) lists Mbara's developments (loss of C1V1, vowel umlaut, metathesis of V1 with C2, lenition, phonotactics) with no stress item. The only Mbara-specific prosodic evidence is seven phonetic forms on p.66 with an acute on the first or only vowel: [kʷár] 'yamstick', [ndé·] 'sun', [mówatʰ] 'axe', [ndʷí] 'food', [lé:] 'dog', [mból] 'tongue', [mbó:l] 'chest'; the acute is the thesis's primary-stress mark in practice (Gugu-Badhun forms p.81-82 carry it on the first syllable, matching §3.2 'regular primary stress on the first syllable'), though it is never defined in words. All Mbara forms cited are consonant-initial after C1V1 loss or metathesis, so the marked stress sits on the initial syllable of the modern word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Mbara. (Gugu-Badhun only, p.82: stems of three or more syllables usually have secondary stress on the third syllable; suffixes forming a third syllable usually do not.)
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mbara. (Gugu-Badhun only: /djibíya/ 'whistler duck' stressed on the second syllable for onomatopoeia, p.82.)
new_statements.identity_note: Sutton 1973 treats Mbara (Woolgar River, north of Richmond, Qld; self-name Mbara, Gudjal name Midjamba = 'Gumbulmara') and Yanga as mutually intelligible, grouping them as his 'Gilbert Pama Group' (p.62); Tindale's 'Ngaon' wordlist is taken to be Yanga or Mbara (p.62, 72). The Mbara data are from Sutton's own 1970 fieldwork (a few dozen words); Yanga is known to him only from informant report. The thesis's own phonology chapter (ch.3) describes Gugu-Badhun, not Mbara.

readall_conflicts: One nominal disagreement. Sutton 1973 (p.24) characterises the whole 'aberrant' (initial-dropping) class of north-east Queensland languages, in which he places Mbara (p.27-28, 30, 60-61), as having 'word-stress on non-initial syllables', whereas the catalog (from Goedemans 1998 category I, resting on Breen's 1979 Mbara phonology MS and Sutton's n.d. Yanga-Mbara MS) records fixed initial stress. The disagreement does not survive contact with the Mbara data in the same thesis: every stress-marked Mbara form (p.66) is consonant-initial after C1V1 loss or V1-C2 metathesis and carries the acute on its first or only syllable, so the modern word is initially stressed exactly as the catalog says. The 'non-initial' wording, like Alpher 1976's 'stress the first vowel that follows a consonant' and Dixon 1980 / Blevins 2001's 'stress shifted to the second syllable' (all seen only as second-hand or snippet material held by the project), describes the pre-dropping word or the vowel-initial sub-case that the thesis does not exemplify for Mbara. Sutton 1976 could not be opened (lending-only / search-only), so the primary published description of Mbara stress remains unread.
